newsitem.title: CROATIA: Bosnian Croat warcrimes suspect in Zagreb jail.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Croat warcrimes suspect in Zagreb jail.

text.p: Indicted Bosnian Croat war crimes suspect Pero Skopljak is in custody in a Zagreb jail and is likely to be transferred to the international tribunal in The Hague on Tuesday, court sources told Reuters on Monday.

"I know that one (Bosnian Croat) is here but I cannot give you the name or anything else," a judge at the Zagreb county court said on Monday. He said there were still legal proceedings to go through before the man could be transferred to The Hague.
Other court employees later told Reuters Skopljak was being held at Remetinec jail in a Zagreb suburb and was likely to be flown out to the Netherlands at around midday on Tuesday.
Skopljak was indicted by the Hague tribunal for crimes committed in central Bosnia in 1993.

He was chief of police in the central Bosnian town of Vitez between October 1992 and May 1993. He is accused of detaining Bosnian Moslem civilians, inhumane treatment of detainees, and using them as human shields and for forced labour.
The Hague indictment says "during such time of detention some of them were murdered or otherwise killed".
The most wanted of Bosnian Croat suspects, Dario Kordic, who was a high-ranking politician in Croat-controlled Bosnia, has not been apprehended.

The Hague indictment against Kordic and five others describes attacks on hundreds of Bosnian Moslem houses in the Lasva Valley area of central Bosnia, carried out in order to "kill, terrorise or demoralise" the Moslem population.
The United Nations in Zagreb said they had not been informed that an indicted suspect was currently in custody.

Speculation is mounting throughout the former Yugoslavia that indicted suspects may be forced to surrender to The Hague or may choose to hand themselves over as international pressure intensifies to get the parties to comply with peace agreements.

Foreign Minister Mate Granic told his German counterpart Klaus Kinkel in Frankfurt on Saturday that the so-called 'Vitez group' of seven indicted Bosnian Croats were ready to give themselves up to the tribunal if they were assured of a quick trial.
